haiku-low.q1: No. Cursor updates stay in Redis and never reach the document service or Postgres; those are not touched.
haiku-low.q2: Clients send at most one update per 60 ms, plus a trailing send. The node silently drops any update under 50 ms after the previous accepted one, so it never reaches Redis.
haiku-low.q3: It holds the newest such cursor per connId and draws it only when appliedRev reaches that revision. It draws nothing before then.
haiku-low.q4: It is drawn at transformPosition(pos, rev, appliedRev). If that throws HistoryGone, the caret is dropped until the sender's next update.
haiku-low.q5: Each tab is its own connection; the avatar shows while any tab lives, with the caret of the most recently moved tab. The avatar leaves only when the user's last connection leaves.
haiku-low.q6: Clean tab close: within 2 seconds, in milliseconds expected. Node crash: about 35 seconds worst case, against a 45-second limit.
haiku-low.q7: Per document in Redis: sorted set pexp:{doc} for connections, hash cur:{doc} for cursors, pseq:{doc} counter. Heartbeat renews members every 10 s; keys expire after 60 s.
haiku-low.q8: Every node with local sockets on the doc runs sweep every 5 s, removing expired members and cursors. It publishes leave last=true on pres:{doc}, which nodes forward to their local browsers.
haiku-low.q9: The accepted update is published on pres:{doc}; subscribed nodes forward it to their local browsers. Viewers on the sender's node receive it through the same channel, since that node is also subscribed.
haiku-low.q10: The node subscribes to pres:{doc} before join, and join returns a snapshot with seq. The client drops any join or leave event with seq at or below snapshot.seq.
haiku-low.q11: Each connection's last cursor stays in cur:{doc}, and the join snapshot includes every stored cursor, so idle carets arrive with the snapshot.
haiku-low.q12: Each connection stamps cursors with an increasing counter n. The receiver keeps lastN[connId] and ignores any cursor with n at or below it; Redis applies the same rule.

sonnet.q1: No. Cursor updates are ephemeral and never reach the document service or Postgres; they go only through the node, Redis and pub/sub.
sonnet.q2: A client sends at most one update per 60 ms (plus a trailing send so the final position isn't lost). The node silently drops any update arriving under 50 ms after the previous accepted one for that connection; dropped updates never reach Redis.
sonnet.q3: It does not draw it. It holds the newest such cursor per connId and draws it once its appliedRev reaches that revision.
sonnet.q4: It is drawn at transformPosition(pos, rev, appliedRev). If transformPosition throws HistoryGone (history too old), the caret is dropped until the sender's next update.
sonnet.q5: One avatar per user (added when a join event has first=true), with carets per connection; each avatar shows the caret with the highest ts (most recently moved tab). The avatar is removed only when a leave event has last=true, i.e. when their last connection is gone.
sonnet.q6: Clean tab close: within 2 s (in practice milliseconds). Node crash: within 45 s limit; about 35 s worst case (30 s expiry plus up to 5 s until next sweep).
sonnet.q7: In Redis, shared by all gateway nodes. Granularity is per WebSocket connection (member userId|connId in sorted set pexp:{doc}, cursor per connId in hash cur:{doc}), keyed per document. Freshness: each node's heartbeat every 10 s renews the member's expiry to now+30 s (ZADD XX) and renews key TTLs; keys also have EXPIRE 60 s renewed by every write.
sonnet.q8: The crashed node's members stop being renewed and their scores expire within 30 s. Every surviving node with local sockets on the doc runs the sweep script every 5 s, which removes expired members and cursors and publishes leave (last=true for users with no live member left) on pres:{doc}. Being atomic, only one node publishes each removal; nodes forward the event to their local browsers. If no node has a socket on the doc, the 60 s EXPIRE clears the keys.
sonnet.q9: The node runs the cursor Lua script, which stores the cursor (if n is higher than stored) and publishes a cursor event on pres:{doc} from inside the script. All nodes subscribed to that channel receive it and forward it to their local browsers. The sender's own node is also subscribed and gets it the same way (the document's diagram shows this for join events on the node itself); the document does not describe a separate local shortcut for cursors.
sonnet.q10: The node subscribes to pres:{doc} before running join. Join returns a snapshot atomically with its own publish, including seq (pseq after the join). The client drops any join or leave event with seq <= snapshot.seq since the snapshot already includes it.
sonnet.q11: Each connection's last cursor stays in cur:{doc}, and the join snapshot includes all stored cursors, so idle users' carets arrive in the snapshot.
sonnet.q12: Each connection stamps cursors with a strictly increasing counter n. The receiver keeps lastN[connId] and ignores any cursor with n <= lastN (late, out-of-order, duplicates, or a held cursor replaced by a newer one). Redis applies the same rule to stored cursors. Cursors for a connId that has already left are also ignored.
